topic.title: No Cost EMI
topic.claim: No Cost EMI moves the cost to a column you don't read, and what sellers really buy is your comparison.
topic.moment: The green 'No Cost EMI' line under the price at checkout in the festive sale.

turn.actually: the interest is still charged and offset by a discount; GST on the interest, fees and lost discounts remain

topic.payoff: When a price gets broken into months, the full number was losing the argument.

paragraphs: Nobody gives you a free loan in a festive sale. "No Cost EMI" just moves the cost to a column you don't read.
slides.why_swipe: a claim that the line everyone trusts hides something; which column?

paragraphs: iPhone 17, 256GB. ₹86,999 in Big Billion Days earlier this month. Right under it: No Cost EMI.
slides.why_swipe: the reader feels the switch in their own head; how is it no cost?

paragraphs: On most card EMIs, the bank still charges interest. The seller knocks the same amount off the price upfront. Net zero, on paper.
Off paper, your card statement often shows 18% GST on that interest, and many banks add a processing fee.
slides.why_swipe: the costs are out; why would anyone pay your interest?

paragraphs: Ask anyone on the selling side: it isn't charity. The brand, the platform or the bank pays that interest because EMI makes more people buy, and buy bigger.
slides.why_swipe: the scale explains the motive; what is the money buying?

big.label: online festive sales in the first two days; phones nearly 40%

paragraphs: What they're paying for is how the price feels.
₹86,999 feels like a decision. ₹14,500 feels like one more monthly bill, and next to a salary almost any monthly bill looks small.
**When a price gets broken into months, the full number was losing the argument.**
slides.why_swipe: the idea has landed; the last slide makes it personal

paragraphs: Someone is reading this right now on a phone with four payments left.

mechanism.broken_premise: None. Every premise checks out against primary sources. The only slight overstatement is 'many banks add a processing fee' on No Cost EMI specifically — for genuine No-Cost EMI the processing fee is frequently waived or token (₹0–₹199), though its GST and the GST on the notional interest are real and customer-borne. This doesn't break the argument.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: The bank does lend at a real rate (~13–16% p.a.) and books an interest component; the merchant/brand/platform funds an equal upfront discount so the financed interest nets to roughly zero for the buyer — RBI's 2013 circular confirms 'zero percent interest is non-existent' and that the cost is simply repackaged (historically as a hidden processing fee or dealer discount). What the discount does NOT cover is 18% GST on that interest, which uniquely applies to credit-card EMI interest (ordinary loan interest is GST-exempt, but credit-card services are carved out), plus any processing fee and its GST — all billed to the customer. Sellers absorb the residual because EMI reliably lifts conversion and basket size, so the framing pays for itself.

sources.quote: In the zero percent EMI schemes offered on credit card outstandings, the interest element is often camouflaged and passed on to the customer in the form of processing fee... the very concept of zero percent interest is non-existent.
the seller covers the interest amount, but not the GST liability on that interest... This GST is not part of the discount and is not visible in the product price. It gets added to your monthly EMI.
NCEMI means there's no additional interest charged to you. But we're a bank and we can't lend money for free... Only credit card interest is charged GST, and this is not applicable to any other loan.
the customer paid the sticker price for the goods while the bank got a dealer-discount that was opaque to the customer and effectively, it was the interest charged by the bank.
